The Copper Causeway
Edition B. An original fictional revision written as a research fixture.

I. The Departure
Mara, the ferry keeper, carried a copper cup, a spool of white thread, and a sealed letter across the marsh. Her brother Iven stayed at the village forge. Before leaving, Mara struck the bronze bell three times. The first strike called the ferryman, the second warned the reed cutters, and the third was the signal she and Iven had agreed upon.

At the western landing, Mara tied a green cord to the willow. She left the copper cup beneath the roots for a traveler who would arrive after sunset. No one drank from the cup in this scene.

II. The Toll
The gatekeeper demanded the sealed letter as a toll. Mara instead offered the spool of white thread. The gatekeeper accepted it because he needed to mend the net across the channel. He did not open the letter or learn who had written it.

The gatekeeper declared, "No boat has crossed this channel in seven winters." The narrator immediately described fresh oar marks in the mud beside his hut. The gatekeeper's claim is a statement by a character, not an independently established history of the channel.

III. The Shelter
An unnamed traveler reached the willow after sunset and found the copper cup. She filled it with rainwater and gave it to a wounded fox. She then placed the empty cup on a stone at the threshold of the abandoned watchhouse. Mara did not witness these actions.

IV. The Return
Mara returned before dawn with the sealed letter still unopened. At the watchhouse, she recognized the copper cup by a crescent-shaped dent near its handle. The narrator does not identify the sender or recipient of the letter anywhere in this edition.

Mara struck the bronze bell once. Iven came from the forge carrying a covered lantern. He understood the single strike as a request for company, whereas the three departure strikes had divided a public warning from a private signal.

V. The Account
At the village table, the gatekeeper repeated his claim about seven winters. The unnamed traveler answered by setting a wet oar beside his chair. The narrator closes with the unopened letter beside the copper cup; neither object is explicitly assigned a single symbolic meaning.
